nodes.name: Feder-Vardi dichotomy conjecture
nodes.statement: Classifying the complexity of \emph{all} valued constraint languages is a challenging task as it includes as a special case the classification of $\{0,\infty\}$-valued languages (i.e., constraint languages), which would answer the conjecture of Feder and Vardi~\cite{Feder98:monotone}, which asserts that every constraint language is either tractable or NP-hard, and its algebraic refinement, which specifies the precise boundary between tractable and NP-hard languages~\cite{Bulatov05:classifying}.
nodes.statement_short: Every constraint language is either tractable or NP-hard (Feder-Vardi), with an algebraic refinement of the boundary.
conclusions: every constraint language is either tractable or NP-hard

nodes.name: Domain $D$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, let $D$ be a fixed finite set of size at least two.

nodes.name: Relation
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary \emph{relation} over $D$ is any mapping $\phi:D^m\to\{c,\infty\}$ for some $c\in\mathbb{Q}$. We denote by ${\bf R}_D^{(m)}$ the set of all $m$-ary relations and let ${\bf R}_D=\bigcup_{m\geq 1}{{\bf R}_D^{(m)}}$.
nodes.label: def:rel

nodes.name: Relations as subsets
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary relation over $D$ is commonly defined as a subset of $D^m$. Note that Definition~\ref{def:rel} is equivalent to the standard definition as any subset of $D^m$ can be associated with the set $\{\tup{x}\in D^m\:|\:\phi(\tup{x})<\infty\}$. Consequently, we shall use both definitions interchangeably.

nodes.name: Tuple entry $\tup{x}[i]$
nodes.statement: Given an $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we denote its $i$th entry by $\tup{x}[i]$ for $1\leq i\leq m$.

nodes.name: Extended rationals
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}=\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ denote the set of rational numbers with (positive) infinity.

nodes.name: Weighted relation
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary \emph{weighted relation}\footnote{In some paper weighted relations are called cost functions.} over $D$ is any mapping $\phi:D^m\to\ensuremath{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}$. We denote by ${\bf \Phi}_D^{(m)}$ the set of all $m$-ary weighted relations and let ${\bf \Phi}_D=\bigcup_{m\ge 1}{{\bf \Phi}_D^{(m)}}$.
nodes.label: def:wrel

nodes.name: Relations are weighted relations
nodes.statement: From Definition~\ref{def:wrel} we have that relations are a special type of weighted relations.

nodes.name: Unweighted relation
nodes.statement: If needed we call a weighted relation \emph{unweighted} to emphasise the fact that $\phi$ is a relation.

nodes.name: Binary equality relation
nodes.statement: An important example of a (weighted) relation is the binary equality $\phi_=$ on $D$: $\phi_=(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$ and $\phi_=(x,y)=\infty$ if $x\neq y$.

nodes.name: Feasibility relation
nodes.statement: For any $m$-ary weighted relation $\phi\in{\bf \Phi}_D^{(m)}$, we denote by $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)=\{\tup{x}\in D^m\:|\:\phi(\tup{x})<\infty\}\in{\bf R}_D^{(m)}$ the underlying \emph{feasibility relation}.

nodes.name: Finite-valued weighted relation
nodes.statement: A weighted relation $\phi:D^m\to\ensuremath{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}$ is called \emph{finite-valued} if $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)=D^m$.

nodes.name: Valued constraint
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{x_1,\ldots, x_n\}$ be a set of variables. A \emph{valued constraint} over $V$ is an expression of the form $\phi(\tup{x})$ where $\phi\in {\bf \Phi}_D^{(m)}$ and $\tup{x}\in V^m$. The number $m$ is called the \emph{arity} of the constraint, the weighted relation $\phi$ is called the \emph{constraint weighted relation}, and the tuple $\tup{x}$ the \emph{scope} of the constraint.
nodes.statement_short: A valued constraint is $\phi(\mathbf{x})$ with weighted relation $\phi$ and scope tuple $\mathbf{x}$; defines arity and scope.

nodes.name: Domain and labels
nodes.statement: We call $D$ the \emph{domain}, the elements of $D$ \emph{labels} (for variables), and say that the weighted relation in ${\bf \Phi}_D$ take \emph{values}.

nodes.name: Valued constraint satisfaction problem (VCSP)
nodes.statement: An instance of the \emph{valued constraint satisfaction problem} (VCSP) is specified by a finite set $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ of variables, a finite set $D$ of labels, and an \emph{objective function} $\ensuremath{I}$ expressed as follows: \begin{equation} \ensuremath{I}(x_1,\ldots, x_n)=\sum_{i=1}^q{\phi_i(\tup{x}_i)}\,, \end{equation} where each $\phi_i(\tup{x}_i)$, $1\le i\le q$, is a valued constraint over $V$. Each constraint can appear multiple times in $\ensuremath{I}$. The goal is to find an \emph{assignment} (or a \emph{labelling}) of labels to the variables that minimises $\ensuremath{I}$.
nodes.statement_short: Given variables, labels and a sum of valued constraints, find a labelling minimising the objective.

nodes.name: Equation (1): VCSP objective function
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{I}(x_1,\ldots, x_n)=\sum_{i=1}^q{\phi_i(\tup{x}_i)}\,,
nodes.label: eq:sepfun

nodes.name: CSP as special case of VCSP
nodes.statement: CSPs are a special case of VCSPs with (unweighted) relations with the goal to determine the existence of a feasible solution.

nodes.name: Max-Cut as a VCSP
nodes.statement: The \textsc{Max-Cut} problem for a graph is to find a cut with the largest possible size. This problem is NP-hard~\cite{Garey79:intractability} and equivalent to the \textsc{Min-UnCut} problem with respect to exact solvability. For a graph $(V,E)$ with $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, this problem can be expressed as the VCSP instance $\ensuremath{I}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E} \phi_{\sf xor}(x_i,x_j)$ over the Boolean domain $D=\{0,1\}$, where $\phi_{\sf xor}:\{0,1\}^2\to\ensuremath{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}$ is defined by $\phi_{\sf xor}(x,y)=1$ if $x=y$ and $\phi_{\sf xor}(x,y)=0$ if $x\neq y$.
nodes.statement_short: Max-Cut is the VCSP over $\{0,1\}$ with the binary weighted relation $\phi_{\sf xor}$ on each edge; NP-hard.
nodes.label: ex:maxcut

nodes.name: Valued constraint language
nodes.statement: Any set $\Gamma\subseteq{\bf \Phi}_D$ is called a \emph{valued constraint language}\footnote{A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is sometimes called \emph{general-valued} to emphasise the fact that weighted relations from $\Gamma$ are not necessarily finite-valued.} over $D$, or simply a \emph{language}. We will denote by $\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma)$ the class of all VCSP instances in which the constraint weighted relations are all contained in $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Tractable valued constraint language
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is called \emph{tractable} if $\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma')$ can be solved (to optimality) in polynomial time for every finite subset $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$ is called \emph{intractable} if $\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma')$ is NP-hard for some finite $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma$ is tractable if every finite subset gives a polynomial-time VCSP, intractable if some finite subset is NP-hard.

nodes.name: Finite-valued constraint language
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language is called \emph{finite-valued} if every weighted relation $\phi$ from the language is finite-valued.
differentia: every weighted relation $\phi$ from the language is finite-valued

nodes.name: Intractability of $\phi_{\sf xor}$
nodes.statement: Example~\ref{ex:maxcut} shows that the finite-valued constraint language $\{\phi_{\sf xor}\}$ is intractable.
conclusions: the finite-valued constraint language $\{\phi_{\sf xor}\}$ is intractable

nodes.name: Feasibility relations of a language
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathrm{Feas}(\Gamma)=\{{Feas}(\phi)\:|\:\phi\in\Gamma\}$ the set of underlying relations of all weighted relations from $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Expressibility
nodes.statement: We say that an $m$-ary weighted relation $\phi$ is \emph{expressible} over a valued constraint language $\Gamma$ if there exists a VCSP instance $\ensuremath{I} \in \mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma)$ with variables $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m\}$, such that \begin{equation} \phi(y_1,\ldots,y_m) = \min_{x_1\in D,\ldots,x_n\in D}\ensuremath{I}(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.label: def:expres

nodes.name: Equation (2): Expressibility by minimisation
nodes.statement: \phi(y_1,\ldots,y_m) = \min_{x_1\in D,\ldots,x_n\in D}\ensuremath{I}(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\,.

nodes.name: Closed under expressibility
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is \emph{closed under expressibility} if every weighted relation $\phi$ expressible over $\Gamma$ belongs to $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma \subseteq {\bf \Phi}_D$ is called a \emph{weighted relational clone} if it contains the binary equality relation $\phi_=$ on $D$ and is closed under expressibility, scaling by non-negative rational constants (where we define $0\cdot\infty=\infty$), and addition of rational constants. For any $\Gamma$, we define $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$ to be the smallest weighted relational clone containing $\Gamma$.
differentia: it contains the binary equality relation $\phi_=$ on $D$
closed under expressibility, scaling by non-negative rational constants
nodes.statement_short: A weighted relational clone contains $\phi_=$ and is closed under expressibility, non-negative scaling and adding constants; defines $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$.
nodes.label: defn:wrelclone

nodes.name: Weighted relational clones contain feasibility relations
nodes.statement: Note that for any weighted relational clone $\Gamma$ if $\phi\in\Gamma$ then $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)\in\Gamma$ as $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)=0\phi$.
assumptions: $\Gamma$
$\phi\in\Gamma$

nodes.name: Relational clone
nodes.statement: A \emph{relational clone} is a weighted relational clone containing only (unweighted) relations.\footnote{Equivalently, a set of relations containing the binary equality relation and closed under conjunction and existential quantification.} For a set of relations $\Gamma$, we denote by $\mathrm{RelClone}(\Gamma)$ the smallest relational clone containing $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Tractability is preserved by weighted relational clone closure
nodes.statement: It has been shown that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$ is tractable~\cite{cccjz13:sicomp}.
conclusions: $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$ is tractable

nodes.name: Operation
nodes.statement: Any mapping $f:D^k\rightarrow D$ is called a $k$-ary \emph{operation}.

nodes.name: Coordinatewise application of an operation
nodes.statement: We will apply a $k$-ary operation $f$ to $k$ $m$-tuples $\tup{x_1},\ldots,\tup{x_k}\in D^m$ coordinatewise, that is, \begin{equation} f(\tup{x_1},\ldots,\tup{x_k})=(f(\tup{x_1}[1],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[1]),\ldots,f(\tup{x_1}[m],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[m]))\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (3): Coordinatewise application
nodes.statement: f(\tup{x_1},\ldots,\tup{x_k})=(f(\tup{x_1}[1],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[1]),\ldots,f(\tup{x_1}[m],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[m]))\,.

nodes.name: Polymorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation on $D$ and let $f$ be a $k$-ary operation on $D$. Then $f$ is a \emph{polymorphism} of $\phi$ if, for any $\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k} \in D^m$ with $\tup{x_i}\in{Feas}(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have that $f(\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k})\in{Feas}(\phi)$. For any valued constraint language $\Gamma$ over a set $D$, we denote by $\mathrm{Pol}(\Gamma)$ the set of all operations on $D$ which are polymorphisms of all $\phi \in \Gamma$. We write $\mathrm{Pol}(\phi)$ for $\mathrm{Pol}(\{\phi\})$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$ if applying $f$ to feasible tuples gives a feasible tuple; $\mathrm{Pol}(\Gamma)$ collects common polymorphisms.
nodes.label: def:pol

nodes.name: Projection
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{projection} is an operation of the form $\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=x_i$ for some $1\leq i\leq k$.

nodes.name: Projections are polymorphisms
nodes.statement: Projections are (trivial) polymorphisms of all valued constraint languages.
conclusions: Projections are (trivial) polymorphisms of all valued constraint languages.

nodes.name: Superposition of operations
nodes.statement: The \emph{superposition} of a $k$-ary operation $f:D^k\rightarrow D$ with $k$ $\ell$-ary operations $g_i:D^\ell\rightarrow D$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ is the $\ell$-ary function $f[g_1,\ldots,g_k]:D^\ell\to D$ defined by \begin{equation} f[g_1,\ldots,g_k](x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)=f(g_1(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell),\ldots,g_k(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell))\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (4): Superposition of operations
nodes.statement: f[g_1,\ldots,g_k](x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)=f(g_1(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell),\ldots,g_k(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell))\,.

nodes.name: Clone
nodes.statement: A \emph{clone} of operations, $C$, is a set of operations on $D$ that contains all projections and is closed under superposition. The $k$-ary operations in a clone $C$ will be denoted by $C^{(k)}$.
nodes.label: def:clone

nodes.name: Clones of projections and of all operations
nodes.statement: For any $D$, let $\mathbf{J}_D$ be the set of all projections on $D$ and $\mathcal{O}_D$ be the set of all operations on $D$. By Definition~\ref{def:clone}, both $\mathbf{J}_D$ and $\mathcal{O}_D$ are clones.
nodes.label: ex:clone

nodes.name: Polymorphisms form a clone
nodes.statement: It is well known that $\mathrm{Pol}(\Gamma)$ is a clone for all valued constraint languages $\Gamma$~\cite{Denecke-Wismath02}.
assumptions: valued constraint languages $\Gamma$

nodes.name: Weighting
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{weighting} of a clone $C$ is a function $\omega : C^{(k)} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ such that $\omega(f) < 0$ only if $f$ is a projection and \begin{equation} \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\ =\ 0\,. \end{equation} We define ${\rm supp}(\omega)=\{f\in C^{(k)}\:|\:\omega(f)>0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: A $k$-ary weighting of clone $C$ assigns rationals to $k$-ary operations, summing to zero, negative only on projections; defines its support.
nodes.label: defn:wop

nodes.name: Equation (5): Weighting sums to zero
nodes.statement: \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\ =\ 0\,.
nodes.label: ineq:weightingzero

nodes.name: Superposition of a weighting
nodes.statement: For any clone $C$, any $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ of $C$, and any $g_1,\ldots,g_k \in C^{(\ell)}$, the \emph{superposition} of $\omega$ and $g_1,\ldots,g_k$, is the function $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]: C^{(\ell)} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ defined by \begin{equation} \omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k](f') = \sum_{\{f \in C^{(k)}\:|\:f[g_1,\ldots,g_k] = f'\}}\omega(f)\,. \end{equation} If $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{ineq:weightingzero} then so does $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]$. If the result of a superposition is a valid weighting (that is, negative weights are only assigned to projections) then that superposition will be called a \emph{proper} superposition.
nodes.statement_short: $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]$ pushes the weight of each $f$ onto $f[g_1,\ldots,g_k]$; it is proper if the result is a valid weighting.
nodes.label: defn:wp_trans

nodes.name: Equation (6): Superposition of a weighting
nodes.statement: \omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k](f') = \sum_{\{f \in C^{(k)}\:|\:f[g_1,\ldots,g_k] = f'\}}\omega(f)\,.

nodes.name: Superposition of a weighting as matrix multiplication
nodes.statement: We remark that the superposition (of an operation with other operations) is also known as composition. On the other hand, the superposition of a $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ with $k$ $\ell$-ary operations $g_1,\ldots,g_k$ can be seen as multiplying $\omega$, seen as a (row) vector, by a matrix with rows indexed by $k$-ary operations and columns indexed by $\ell$-ary operations; given a row operation $f$ and a column operation $f'$ the corresponding entry in the matrix is 1 if $f[g_1,\ldots,g_k]=f'$ and 0 otherwise. The result of this matrix multiplication is a vector of weights assigned to $\ell$-ary operations.
nodes.statement_short: Superposing a weighting with operations is multiplying its weight vector by a 0/1 matrix indexed by $k$-ary and $\ell$-ary operations.

nodes.name: Weighted clone
nodes.statement: A \emph{weighted clone}, $W$, is a non-empty set of weightings of some fixed clone $C$, called the \emph{support clone} of $W$, which is closed under nonnegative scaling, addition of weightings of equal arity, and proper superposition with operations from $C$. We define ${\rm supp}(W)=\bigcup_{\omega\in W}{\rm supp}(\omega)$.
nodes.genus: non-empty set of weightings of some fixed clone $C$
differentia: closed under nonnegative scaling, addition of weightings of equal arity, and proper superposition with operations from $C$
nodes.label: defn:wclone

nodes.name: Zero-valued and full weighted clones
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a clone. We give examples of two weighted clones with support clone $C$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathbf{W}_C^0$ is the zero-valued weighted clone, that is, the weighted clone containing, for each arity $k$, a weighting $\omega_k\in\mathbf{W}_C^0$ with $\omega_k(f)=0$ for all $f\in C^{(k)}$. \item $\mathbf{W}_C$ is the weighted clone containing all possible weightings of $C$. \end{enumerate} By Definition~\ref{ex:wclones}, weighted clones are closed under nonnegative scaling. Consequently, by scaling by zero, any weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$ contains $\mathbf{W}_C^0$, which is the inclusion-wise smallest weighted clone with support clone $C$. On the other hand, $\mathbf{W}_C$ is the inclusion-wise largest weighted clone with support clone $C$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{W}_C^0$ (all-zero weightings) and $\mathbf{W}_C$ (all weightings) are the smallest and largest weighted clones with support clone $C$.
nodes.label: ex:wclones

nodes.name: Support of a weighted clone with projections is a clone
nodes.statement: It is easy to show that ${\rm supp}(W)\cup\mathbf{J}_D$ is a clone for any weighted clone $W$ defined on $D$~\cite{cccjz13:sicomp}, see also~\cite{Kozik15:icalp,tz15:icalp}.
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Creed, Jeavons, Zivny 2013 (SICOMP); Kozik & Ochremiak 2015; Thapper & Zivny 2015
assumptions: any weighted clone $W$ defined on $D$

nodes.name: Weighted polymorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation on $D$ and let $\omega$ be a $k$-ary weighting of a clone $C$ of operations on $D$. We call $\omega$ a \emph{weighted polymorphism} of $\phi$ if $C\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}(\phi)$ and for any $\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k \in D^m$ with $\tup{x}_i\in{Feas}(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have \begin{equation} \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)) \ \leq\ 0\,. \end{equation} If $\omega$ is a weighted polymorphism of $\phi$ we say that $\phi$ is \emph{improved} by $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: $\omega$ is a weighted polymorphism of $\phi$ if $C\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}(\phi)$ and the $\omega$-weighted sum of $\phi$ over images of feasible tuples is $\le 0$.
nodes.label: def:wp

nodes.name: Equation (7): Weighted polymorphism inequality
nodes.statement: \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)) \ \leq\ 0\,.
nodes.label: eq:WPOL

nodes.name: Submodular functions
nodes.statement: Consider the class of submodular functions~\cite{Nemhauser88:optimization}. These are precisely the functions $\phi$ defined on $D=\{0,1\}$ satisfying $\phi(\min(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2)) + \phi(\max(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2)) - \phi(\tup{x}_1) - \phi(\tup{x}_2) \leq 0$, where $\min$ and $\max$ are the two binary operations that return the smaller and larger of its two arguments respectively with respect to the usual order $0<1$. In other words, the set of submodular functions is the set of weighted relations with a binary weighted polymorphism $\omega_{sub}$ defined by: $\omega_{sub}(f)=-1$ if $f \in \{e_1^{(2)},e_2^{(2)}\}$, $\omega_{sub}(f)=+1$ if $f \in \{\min,\max\}$, and $\omega_{sub}(f)=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Submodular functions on $\{0,1\}$ are exactly those with the binary weighted polymorphism $\omega_{sub}$ (+1 on min, max; -1 on projections).

nodes.name: Weighted polymorphisms of a language
nodes.statement: For any $\Gamma \subseteq {\bf \Phi}_D$, we define $\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$ to be the set of all weightings of $\mathrm{Pol}(\Gamma)$ which are weighted polymorphisms of all weighted relations $\phi \in \Gamma$. We write $\mathrm{wPol}(\phi)$ for $\mathrm{wPol}(\{\phi\})$.

nodes.name: All weightings on $D$
nodes.statement: We define ${\bf W}_D$ to be the union of the sets ${\bf W}_C$ over all clones $C$ on $D$.

nodes.name: Extending weightings to a common clone
nodes.statement: Any $W \subseteq {\bf W}_D$ may contain weightings of \emph{different} clones over $D$. We can then extend each of these weightings with zeros, as necessary, so that they are weightings of the same clone $C$, where $C$ is the smallest clone containing all the clones associated with weightings in $W$.

nodes.name: Weighted clone generated by a set
nodes.statement: We define $\mathrm{wClone}(W)$ to be the smallest weighted clone containing this set of extended weightings obtained from $W$.

nodes.name: Imp
nodes.statement: For any $W \subseteq {\bf W}_D$, we denote by $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ the set of all weighted relations in ${\bf \Phi}_D$ which are improved by all weightings $\omega \in W$.

nodes.name: Imp of the zero and full weighted clones of projections
nodes.statement: Every weighting in $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D}^0$ is a weighted polymorphism of any possible weighted relation. Hence $\mathrm{Imp}(\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D}^0)={\bf \Phi}_D$. The weighted relations that are improved by all weightings are precisely those which take at most one value. Hence $\mathrm{Imp}(\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D})={\bf R}_D$.

nodes.name: Tractable weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is called \emph{tractable} if $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ is tractable, and intractable if $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ is intractable.

nodes.name: Galois connection between weighted relational clones and weighted clones
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{enumerate} \item For any finite $D$ and any finite $\Gamma \subseteq {\bf \Phi}_D$, $\mathrm{Imp}(\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)) = \mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$. \item For any finite $D$ and any finite $W\subseteq {\bf W}_D$, $\mathrm{wPol}(\mathrm{Imp}(W)) = \mathrm{wClone}(W)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: For any finite $D$ and any finite $\Gamma \subseteq {\bf \Phi}_D$
For any finite $D$ and any finite $W\subseteq {\bf W}_D$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Imp}\circ\mathrm{wPol}$ is the weighted relational clone closure and $\mathrm{wPol}\circ\mathrm{Imp}$ the weighted clone closure.
nodes.label: thm:wgc

nodes.name: Positive weighting
nodes.statement: A weighting is called \emph{positive} if it assigns positive weight to at least one operation that is not a projection.
differentia: assigns positive weight to at least one operation that is not a projection

nodes.name: Positive weightings are necessary for tractability
nodes.statement: Positive weightings are necessary for tractability: any tractable weighted clone $W$ contains a positive weighting~\cite[Corollary 7.4]{cccjz13:sicomp}.
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Creed, Jeavons, Zivny 2013 (SICOMP), Corollary 7.4
assumptions: any tractable weighted clone $W$

nodes.name: Standing assumption: positive weighting
nodes.statement: Consequently, throughout this paper we will be only concerned with weighted clones that contain a positive weighting.

nodes.name: Sharp operation
nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 2$, a $k$-ary operation $f$ is called \emph{sharp} if $f$ is not a projection, but the operation obtained by equating any two inputs in $f$ is a projection~\cite{Csakany05:minimal}.
differentia: the operation obtained by equating any two inputs in $f$ is a projection

nodes.name: Idempotent operation
nodes.statement: All sharp operations must satisfy the identity $f(x,x,\ldots,x) = x$; such operations are called \emph{idempotent}.

nodes.name: Eight types of ternary sharp operations
nodes.statement: Ternary sharp operations may be classified according to their labels on tuples of the form $(x,x,y), (x,y,x)$ and $(y,x,x)$, which must be equal to either $x$ or $y$. There are precisely $8$ possibilities, as listed in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3}.
assumptions: Ternary sharp operations
nodes.statement_short: Ternary sharp operations fall into 8 types by their values on $(x,x,y),(x,y,x),(y,x,x)$ (Table 1).

nodes.name: Majority operation
nodes.statement: The first column in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} corresponds to operations that satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=x$ for all $x,y\in D$; such operations are called \emph{majority} operations.

nodes.name: Minority operation
nodes.statement: The last column in the table corresponds to operations that satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y\in D$; such operations are called \emph{minority} operations.

nodes.name: Pixley operation
nodes.statement: Columns 5, 6, and 7 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} correspond to operations that satisfy the identities $f(y,y,x) = f(x,y,x) = f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y \in D$ (up to permutations of inputs); such operations are called \emph{Pixley} operations~\cite{Csakany05:minimal}.

nodes.name: Semiprojection
nodes.statement: For any $k \geq 3$, a $k$-ary operation $f$ is called a \emph{semiprojection} if it is not a projection, but there is an index $1\leq i \leq k$ such that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i$ for all $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in D$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ are not pairwise distinct. In other words, a semiprojection is a particular form of sharp operation where the operation obtained by equating any two inputs is always the \emph{same} projection.
differentia: there is an index $1\leq i \leq k$ such that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i$ for all $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in D$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ are not pairwise distinct

nodes.name: Swierczkowski's Lemma
nodes.statement: The only sharp operations of arity $k\geq 4$ are semiprojections.
assumptions: sharp operations of arity $k\geq 4$
nodes.label: lem:swier

nodes.name: Cyclic permutations
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathrm{Cycl}_k$ the set of $k$ cyclic permutations on $\{1,\ldots,k\}$.

nodes.name: Composition of permutations
nodes.statement: We denote by $\circ$ the composition of two permutations, that is, for any $\sigma,\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$ we have $\sigma\circ\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$ is defined by $\sigma\circ\pi(x)=\sigma(\pi(x))$.

nodes.name: Permuted operation $f^\pi$
nodes.statement: For a $k$-ary operation $f$ and a permutation $\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$ we will denote by $f^\pi$ the operation $f^\pi=f[\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]$, that is, $f^\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)})$.

nodes.name: Cyclic symmetrisation of a positive weighting
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone and $\omega\in W$ a positive $k$-ary weighting. Then there is a positive $k$-ary weighting $\mu\in W$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $\displaystyle{\rm supp}(\mu)=\bigcup_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\bigcup_{\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k} f^\pi$; \item $\mu(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$; \item $\mu(f)=\mu(f^\pi)$ for every $f\in{\rm supp}(\mu)$ and $\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone and $\omega\in W$ a positive $k$-ary weighting.
conclusions: there is a positive $k$-ary weighting $\mu\in W$
nodes.statement_short: Any positive $k$-ary weighting can be replaced by a cyclically symmetric one with weight $-1$ on each projection.
nodes.label: lem:perm

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} \omega'\ =\ \sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k}\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]\,. \end{equation} Let $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ and $\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$. We have \begin{multline} \omega'(f)\ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma}=f$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\circ\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma\circ\pi}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \\ \ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma'\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma'}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ = \ \omega'(f^\pi)\,. \end{multline} Thus $\omega'$ satisfies the first and the third property of the lemma. Since $\omega$ is positive we have that $\sum_{i=1}^k\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i)<0$ and thus, by~\eqref{eq:long}, we have $\omega'(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i)<0$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Let $\omega'(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_1)=w$. By~\eqref{eq:long} again, $\omega'(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i)=w$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Thus $\mu=\frac{1}{w}\omega'$ satisfies all three properties of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the superpositions of $\omega$ with all cyclic permutations of projections, then rescale by the common projection weight.

nodes.name: Equation (8): Cyclic symmetrisation $\omega'$
nodes.statement: \omega'\ =\ \sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k}\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]\,.
nodes.label: ineq:trick

nodes.name: Equation (9): Invariance of $\omega'$ under cyclic permutations
nodes.statement: \omega'(f)\ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma}=f$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\circ\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma\circ\pi}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \\ \ =\ \sum_{g\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma'\in\mathrm{Cycl}_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma'}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ = \ \omega'(f^\pi)\,.
nodes.label: eq:long

nodes.name: Core
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is a \emph{core} if for every unary weighting $\omega\in W$ every operation $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ is bijective. A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is a core if $W=\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$ is a core.
differentia: for every unary weighting $\omega\in W$ every operation $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ is bijective

nodes.name: Reduction to cores
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$. If $\Gamma$ is not a core then there is a core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$.
If $\Gamma$ is not a core
conclusions: there is a core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable
nodes.statement_short: Every non-core valued constraint language has a core language on a subdomain with the same complexity.
nodes.label: thm:squash

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $\omega\in\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$ be a positive unary weighting. By scaling by $1/|\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(1)}_1)|$, we have $\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(1)}_1)=-1$ and thus $\sum_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\omega(f)=1$. For any weighted relation $\phi\in\Gamma$ of arity $m$ and any $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we have $(\ast)$ $\phi(\tup{x})\geq\sum_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}))$. Suppose that $\tup{y}$ is a minimal-cost assignment for $\phi$; that is, $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$ for all $\tup{x}\in D^m$. Then for every $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$, we have $f(\tup{y})$ is also a minimal-cost assignment. Assume for contrary that for some $f'\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$, we have $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))>\phi(\tup{y})$; write $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))=\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon$, where $\epsilon>0$. Then we claim that there is an $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ such that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))<\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts the choice of $\tup{y}$. To prove the claim assume that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))\geq\phi(\tup{y})$ for every $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}$. Hence we get $\sum_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y})) = \sum_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y}))+\omega(f')\phi(f'(\tup{y})) \geq (1-\omega(f')\phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')(\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon) = \phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')\epsilon>\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts $(\ast)$. Consequently, given an instance $I\in\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma)$ and a solution $s$ to $I$, we can take any unary weighting $\omega\in\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$ and any unary operation $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ and get another solution $f(s)$ to $I$; the solution $f(s)$ uses only labels from $f(D)$. Consider a unary non-bijective operation $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ with the minimum $|f(D)|$ over all unary weightings $\omega\in\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$. We denote by $D'=f(D)$ the range of $f$. We denote by $\Gamma'$ language containing the restriction of every $\phi\in\Gamma$ to $D'$. Given any instance $I\in\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma)$ we can create, by replacing each weighted relation $\phi$ in $I$ by $\phi'$, in polynomial time an instance $I'\in\mathrm{VCSP}(\Gamma')$ with the following properties: any solution to $I'$ is also a solution to $I$, and for any solution $s$ to $I$ we have that $f(s)$ is a solution to $I'$. If $\Gamma'$ is not a core we can repeat the same construction with $\Gamma'$.
nodes.statement_short: A unary weighted polymorphism maps optimal assignments to optimal ones; restrict to the smallest image of a non-bijective unary operation and iterate.

nodes.name: Independent result by Kozik and Ochremiak
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:squash} was independently obtained in~\cite{Kozik15:icalp}, where it was also shown that, with respect to tractability, it suffices to restrict to rigid cores.

nodes.name: Rigid core
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is a \emph{rigid core} if the only unary operation in the support clone of $W$ is the unary projection $\ensuremath{e}^{(1)}_1$. A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is a rigid core if $W=\mathrm{wPol}(\Gamma)$ is a rigid core; that is if the only unary polymorphism of $\Gamma$ is $\ensuremath{e}^{(1)}_1$.
differentia: the only unary operation in the support clone of $W$ is the unary projection $\ensuremath{e}^{(1)}_1$

nodes.name: Reduction to rigid cores
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$. If $\Gamma$ is not a rigid core then there is a rigid core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$.
If $\Gamma$ is not a rigid core
conclusions: there is a rigid core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable
nodes.label: thm:rigid

nodes.name: Rigid cores have only idempotent operations
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that a weighted clone $W$ (a valued constraint language $\Gamma$) is a rigid core if and only if all operations in the support clone of $W$ (polymorphisms of $\Gamma$, respectively) are idempotent.
conclusions:
a weighted clone $W$ (a valued constraint language
$\Gamma$) is a rigid core if and only if all operations in the support clone of $W$
(polymorphisms of $\Gamma$, respectively) are idempotent

nodes.name: Creed-Zivny classification of weightings in weighted clones
nodes.statement: ~ Any weighted clone $W$ containing a positive weighting contains a weighting whose support is either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of unary operations that are not projections; or \item a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or \item a set of ternary operations that are majority operations, minority operations, Pixley operations or semiprojections; or \item a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k > 3$). \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Creed & Zivny 2011 (CP'11), Theorem 2; Cohen et al. 2013, Corollary 7.7
assumptions: Any weighted clone $W$ containing a positive weighting
conclusions: contains a weighting whose support is either
nodes.statement_short: Every weighted clone with a positive weighting has a weighting supported on unary non-projections, binary idempotents, ternary sharp operations, or $k$-ary semiprojections.
nodes.label: thm:class1

nodes.name: Main theorem: weightings in rigid-core weighted clones
nodes.statement: Any weighted clone $W$ that is a rigid core and contains a positive weighting also contains a weighting whose support is either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or \item a set of ternary operations that are either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of majority operations; or \item a set of minority operations; or \item a set of majority operations with total weight $2$ and a set of minority operations with total weight $1$; or \end{enumerate} \item a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k \geq 3$). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: thm:class2
assumptions: Any weighted clone $W$ that is a rigid core and contains a positive weighting
conclusions: also contains a weighting whose support is either
nodes.statement_short: A rigid-core weighted clone with a positive weighting has a weighting supported on binary idempotents, majorities, minorities, a 2:1 majority/minority mix, or $k$-ary semiprojections.

nodes.name: Non-strict arity bound in case (3)
nodes.statement: Note that compared to Theorem~\ref{thm:class1} the inequality in case~(3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} is not strict as it includes one of the ternary cases.

nodes.name: Main theorem holds for any support clone
nodes.statement: We remark that Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} holds for \emph{any} weighted clone $W$ with \emph{any} support clone $C$ as long as $W$ contains a positive weighting.

nodes.name: Consequences of the main theorem
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} tells us that (i) Pixley operations are not necessary for tractability, (ii) semiprojections can be separated from the other types of ternary operations, and (iii) the only possible interplay between majority and minority operations, as described in case~(2c) of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}.
nodes.statement_short: Pixley operations are not needed for tractability, semiprojections separate from other ternary types, and majority/minority interact only as in (2c).

nodes.name: Tractability boundary for case (1)
nodes.statement: A weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(1) can lead both to tractable and intractable weighted clones, as the next two examples demonstrate, but the precise boundary of tractability is currently unknown.

nodes.name: Tournament operations
nodes.statement: A binary operation $f:D^2\rightarrow D$ is called conservative if $f(x,y)\in\{x,y\}$ for all $x,y\in D$ and commutative if $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in D$. Moreover, $f$ is called a \emph{tournament} operation if $f$ is both conservative and commutative. Let $W$ be a weighted clone such ${\rm supp}(W)$ contains a tournament operation. Then, by a recent result of the authors~\cite{tz15:icalp}, $W$ is tractable.
nodes.statement_short: A weighted clone whose support contains a conservative commutative (tournament) binary operation is tractable.
nodes.label: ex:TP

nodes.name: Rectangular band
nodes.statement: Let $D=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $f$ be a binary operation defined by Table~\ref{table:bin}. \begin{table}[hbt] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|cccc} \textbf{f} & \textbf{0} & \textbf{1} & \textbf{2} & \textbf{3} \\ \hline \textbf{0} & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{1} & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{2} & 2 & 3 & 2 & 3 \\ \textbf{3} & 2 & 3 & 2 & 3 \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $f$ from Example~\ref{ex:f}.} \end{table} Note that $f$ is an idempotent operation but not a projection. In fact, $f$ is an example of a \emph{rectangular band}~\cite{McKenzie87:algebras}, which is an idempotent and associative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ satisfying $f(x,f(y,z))=f(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z\in D$. Let $W$ be the weighted clone generated by the weighting $\omega$ defined by $\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1)=\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2)=-1$ and $\omega(f)=+2$. It is known that $W$ is intractable~\cite{Jeavons97:closure,Pearson97:survey}.
nodes.statement_short: A rectangular band on $\{0,1,2,3\}$ gives a binary idempotent weighting generating an intractable weighted clone.
nodes.label: ex:f

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: Let $\omega$ be $k$-ary. Note that if $f$ is a $k$-ary near-unanimity operation then so is $g(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the $k$ projections (and still every $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ is a near-unanimity operation). Let $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in{Feas}(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\mathrm{wPol}(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{y}$ and $\tup{x}_i=\tup{x}$ for all $2\leq i\leq k$, and by~\eqref{eq:defNU}, $-\phi(\tup{y})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{x})+k\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$. By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{x})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{y})+k\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in{Feas}(\phi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrise $\omega$ via Lemma 2, then apply the weighted polymorphism inequality to $(y,x,\ldots,x)$ and $(x,y,\ldots,y)$ to get $\phi(x)=\phi(y)$ on feasible tuples.

nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 7 with tractability of crisp languages having a near-unanimity polymorphism.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: Note that if $f$ is a minority operation then so is $g(x_1,x_2,x_3)=f(x_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)},x_{\pi(3)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,2,3\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three projections (and still every $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ is a minority operation). Let $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in{Feas}(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\mathrm{wPol}(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{x}$ and $\tup{x}_2=\tup{x}_3=\tup{y}$, $-\phi(\tup{x})-2\phi(\tup{y})+3\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$. By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{y})-2\phi(\tup{x})+3\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in{Feas}(\phi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrise $\omega$ via Lemma 2, then apply the weighted polymorphism inequality to $(x,y,y)$ and $(y,x,x)$ to get $\phi(x)=\phi(y)$.

nodes.statement: Since crisp weighted relational clones with a minority polymorphism are tractable~\cite{Jeavons97:closure}, we get the following.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Proposition 8 with tractability of crisp languages having a minority polymorphism.

nodes.name: Multimorphisms
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ is a \emph{multimorphism} if $\omega(f)\in\mathbb{N}$ for all $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ and $\omega(\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$~\cite{Cohen06:complexitysoft}. It has been shown that if a weighted clone $W$ contains a weighting $\omega$ described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) such that $\omega$ is a multimorphism then $W$ is tractable~\cite{kz13:jacm}.
nodes.statement_short: Multimorphisms are integral weightings with $-1$ on each projection; a (2c) multimorphism implies tractability.

nodes.name: Semiprojection weightings alone do not imply tractability
nodes.statement: We show that the weightings described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(3) \emph{alone} are not sufficient for tractability.
assumptions: the weightings described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(3)

nodes.name: Tractability boundary for case (3)
nodes.statement: As in case~(1), the precise boundary of tractability is currently unknown.

nodes.name: Not-All-Equal Satisfiability and semiprojections
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a fixed set with $|D|>2$. Fix two distinct labels from $D$, say $0,1\in D$. Let $\phi$ be the following ternary weighted relation: $\phi(x,y,z)=\infty$ if $\{x,y,z\}=\{0\}$, or $\{x,y,z\}=\{1\}$, or $\{x,y,z\}\neq\{0,1\}$; and $\phi(x,y,z)=0$ otherwise. The weighted relation $\phi$ corresponds to the \textsc{Not-All-Equal Satisfiability} problem~\cite{Garey79:intractability}, which is NP-hard~\cite{Schaefer78:complexity}. It is easy to show that every semiprojection on $D$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$. Take a $k$-ary semiprojection $f$ for some $k\geq 3$ and $\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k\in\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)$. From the definition of $\phi$, we have $\tup{x}_i\in\{0,1\}^3$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Since there are at most two distinct labels in each coordinate, $f(\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)$ reduces to a projection (from the definition of semiprojections) and thus $f$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$ as $f(\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)=\tup{x}_i$ for some $1\leq i\leq k$. Let $C$ be the clone of operations on $D$ generated by all semiprojections on $D$. Let $W=\mathbf{W}_C$ be the weighted clone containing all possible weightings of $C$. In particular, $W$ contains all possible weightings whose support contains only semiprojections. Since $C\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}(\phi)$ and $\phi$ is a relation we have that $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$. Consequently, $W$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: NAE-SAT is preserved by all semiprojections, so the full weighted clone on the semiprojection clone is intractable.

nodes.name: Finite-valued languages correspond to support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$
nodes.statement: Weighted clones corresponding to finite-valued constraint languages (together with the binary equality relation $\phi_=$) are those with support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$.

nodes.name: Argument for support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$
nodes.statement: To see this, we denote, for a clone $C$, by $\mathrm{Inv}(C)$ the relational clone that consists of relations $R$ with $f\in\mathrm{Pol}(R)$ for every $f\in C$. Then, it is well known that $\mathrm{Inv}(\mathcal{O}_D)=\mathrm{RelClone}(\{\phi_=\})$ and observe that $\mathrm{Feas}(\mathrm{Imp}(W))\subseteq\mathrm{Inv}(\mathcal{O}_D)$ for any weighted clone $W$ with support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$.\footnote{More generally, we have $\mathrm{Feas}(\mathrm{Imp}(W))=\mathrm{Inv}(C)$ for any nonempty weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$. On the one hand, if $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ then, by Definition~\ref{def:wp}, $C\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}(\phi)$, which implies $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)\in\mathrm{Inv}(\mathrm{Pol}(\phi))\subseteq\mathrm{Inv}(C)$. On the other hand, if $R\in\mathrm{Inv}(C)$ then $C\subseteq\mathrm{Pol}(R)$. Since $R$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:WPOL} we have $R\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$.}
nodes.statement_short: Use $\mathrm{Inv}(\mathcal{O}_D)=\mathrm{RelClone}(\{\phi_=\})$ and $\mathrm{Feas}(\mathrm{Imp}(W))\subseteq\mathrm{Inv}(C)$.

nodes.name: Finite-valued case (2a), (2b) is tractable

Similarly, if $W$ contains a weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2b) then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:minority}, $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ is crisp and thus every $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ can be written as the addition of a rational constant to a weighted relation in $\mathcal{R}$. Hence $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ is tractable.
nodes.statement_short: In the finite-valued case, (2a) and (2b) weightings make $\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ crisp and hence constants plus relations in $\mathcal{R}$, so tractable.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 10
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume the weighting assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three projections and still is as described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c). An $m$-ary relation $R$ on $D$ is called trivial if $R=D^m$. First we show than any relation $R\in\mathcal{R}$ can be expressed as a sum of unary relations, trivial relations, and $\phi_=$. The claim holds true for the generators of $\mathcal{R}$, that is, for $\phi_=$ and $\phi_d$ for all $d\in D$. Next, if $R=R_1\wedge R_2$ and the claim holds true for both $R_1$ and $R_2$ the it also holds true for $R$. Finally, let $R=\exists x R'$ and assume that $R'$ satisfies the claim. If $x$ appears in some $\phi_=$ in $R'$, say $\phi_=(x,x')$, then we can replace all occurrences of $x$ by $x'$. Otherwise, $x$ appears only in constant and trivial relations in $R'$. If the conjunction of the unary relations that $x$ appears in is empty then the claim holds trivially. Otherwise, we can replace $x$ by any other variable. Consequently, for any $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$, $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)$ can be written as a sum of unary relations, trivial relations, and $\phi_=$. Observe that any $\phi$ with $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)=\phi_=$ can be written as a sum of $\phi_=$ and the unary weighted relation $\phi'(x)=\phi(x,x)$. Thus, it remains to show that any $\phi\in\mathrm{Imp}(W)$ with $\mathrm{Feas}(\phi)$ being a trivial relation can be written as a sum of unary weighted relations. For any $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we will write $\tup{x}[i\leftarrow d]$ to denote the tuple with $d\in D$ {substituted} at position $i$. In other words, $\tup{x}[i\leftarrow d]$ is the $m$-tuple identical to $\tup{x}$ except (possibly) at position $i$, where it is equal to $d$. We will use~\cite[Lemma~6.23]{Cohen06:complexitysoft} which says that a weighted relation $\phi:D^m\to\mbox{$\mathbb Q$}$ can be expressed as a sum of unary weighted relations if and only if, for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ and all $1\leq i\leq m$, we have \begin{equation} \phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y}) = \phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow \tup{y}[i]]) + \phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow \tup{x}[i]])\,. \end{equation} Take any $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ and $1\leq i\leq m$. Let $a=\tup{x}[i]$ and $b=\tup{y}[i]$. Now consider the tuples $\tup{x}$, $\tup{x}[i\leftarrow b]$, and $\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]$. By applying the weighting from the statement of the proposition as in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $\phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow b])+\phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]) \geq 2\phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y})$ and thus $\phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow b])+\phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]) \geq \phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y})$. Now consider the tuples $\tup{x}$, $\tup{y}$, and $\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]$. By applying the weighting from the statement of the proposition as in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $\phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y})+\phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]) \geq 2\phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]) + \phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow b])$ and thus $\phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y}) \geq \phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow a]) + \phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow b])$.
nodes.statement_short: Structural induction shows feasibility relations decompose into unary, trivial and equality relations; then the (2c) weighting yields the exchange identity of [Cohen et al., Lemma 6.23]. The key step applies the weighting to two triples of tuples to get both inequalities.

nodes.name: Intractable finite-valued weighted clone with binary weighting
nodes.statement: Let $D=\{0,1,2\}$. Recall from Example~\ref{ex:TP} that a binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ is \emph{conservative} if $f(x,y)\in\{x,y\}$ for all $x,y\in D$. For any conservative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ and any 2-element subdomain $\{a,b\}\subseteq D$, the restriction $\Crestrict{f}{\{a,b\}}$ of $f$ onto $\{a,b\}$ behaves either as $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$, $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$, $\min$, or $\max$, where $\min$ and $\max$ are the two operations that return the smaller (larger) of its two arguments with respect to the usual order $0<1<2$, respectively. Consider the operations in Table~\ref{table:w} described by their behaviour on the various 2-element subdomains. \begin{table}[htb] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{lccc|l} $\mathbf{f}$ & \{\textbf{0},\textbf{1}\} & \{\textbf{0},\textbf{2}\} & \{\textbf{1},\textbf{2}\} & $\mathbf{\omega(f)}$\\ \hline $f_1$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ & -0.5 \\ $f_2$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$ & -0.5 \\ $f_3$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ & $\min$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ & 0.5 \\ $f_4$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$ & $\min$ & $\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$ & 0.5 \\ \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $\omega$} \end{table} Note that $f_1=\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_1$ and $f_{2}=\ensuremath{e}^{(2)}_2$. The weighting $\omega$ is defined by the last column of Table~\ref{table:w}. Note that $\omega$ is not commutative. It can be checked that $\omega$ is a weighted polymorphism of the finite-valued weighted relation $\phi : \{0,1,2\} \to \mbox{$\mathbb Q$}$ defined in Table~\ref{table:phi}. \begin{table}[hbt] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $\phi$ & \textbf{0} & \textbf{1} & \textbf{2} \\ \hline \textbf{0} & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{1} & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ \textbf{2} & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $\phi$} \end{table} Now since $\mathrm{argmin} \phi=\{(0,1),(1,0)\}$, we have that $\phi$ satisfies the (MC) condition~\cite{tz13:stoc} and thus can be used to reduce from Max-Cut~\cite{Cohen06:complexitysoft}. Thus, $W=\mathrm{wClone}(\{\omega\})$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: A non-commutative conservative binary weighting on $\{0,1,2\}$ improves a Max-Cut-like finite-valued $\phi$, so its weighted clone is intractable.

\emph{commutative} operations only

assumptions: $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)={\bf \Phi}_D$

nodes.name: Maximal weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: A weighted relational clone $\Gamma\subseteq{\bf \Phi}_D$ is called \emph{maximal} if $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)\neq{\bf \Phi}_D$ but for any $\phi\not\in\Gamma$ we have $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma\cup\{\phi\})={\bf \Phi}_D$.
nodes.label: def:maximal

nodes.name: Maximal languages vs. maximal clones
nodes.statement: It follows that a valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is maximal if and only if the weighted relational clone $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$ is maximal.
conclusions:
a valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is maximal if and only if
the weighted relational clone $\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma)$ is maximal

nodes.name: Maximal relational clone
nodes.statement: As a special case of Definition~\ref{def:maximal}, we get that a relational clone $\Gamma$ is maximal if $\Gamma\neq{\bf R}_D$ but for any $R\in{\bf R}_D$ we have $\mathrm{RelClone}(\Gamma\cup\{R\})={\bf R}_D$.

nodes.name: Minimal weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$ is called \emph{minimal} if $W\neq{\bf W}_C^0$ and every positive weighting $\omega\in W$ satisfies $\mathrm{wClone}(\omega)=W$.

nodes.name: Maximal weighted relational clones correspond to minimal weighted clones
nodes.statement: Maximal weighted relational clones correspond, via the Galois correspondence given in Theorem~\ref{thm:wgc}, to minimal weighted clones.
conclusions:
Maximal weighted relational clones correspond, via the Galois correspondence
given in Theorem~\ref{thm:wgc}, to minimal weighted clones.

nodes.name: Maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones are intractable
nodes.statement: All maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones are intractable.
assumptions: maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: If $\Gamma$ contains all finite-valued weighted relations then it is intractable. Otherwise, there is a finite-valued weighted relation $\phi\not\in\Gamma$. Since $\phi$ is finite-valued we have $\mathrm{Feas}(\Gamma)=\mathrm{Feas}(\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma\cup\{\phi\}))$. But then either $\mathrm{Feas}(\Gamma)=\mathbf{R}_D$, in which case $\Gamma$ is intractable, or $\mathrm{Feas}(\Gamma)=\mathrm{Feas}(\mathrm{wRelClone}(\Gamma\cup\{\phi\}))\neq\mathbf{R}_D$, in which case $\Gamma$ is not maximal.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis: either $\Gamma$ contains all finite-valued weighted relations, or adding a finite-valued one leaves the feasibility relations unchanged, so $\Gamma$ is not maximal unless intractable.

nodes.name: Gordan's Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times m}$ be a matrix. Either $Ax=0$, where $x\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $x\geq 0$ and $x\neq 0$, or $\exists y\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ with $y^{\intercal}A>0$.
assumptions: Let $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times m}$ be a matrix.
conclusions:
Either $Ax=0$, where $x\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $x\geq 0$
and $x\neq 0$, or $\exists y\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ with $y^{\intercal}A>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem of the alternative: $Ax=0$ has a nonzero nonnegative solution or some $y$ has $y^T A>0$.
nodes.label: thm:gordan

nodes.name: Sums of superpositions
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a clone, and let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be weightings of $C$, of arity $k$ and $\ell$ respectively. For any $g_1,\ldots,g_k \in C^{(m)}$ and any $g'_1,\ldots,g'_\ell \in C^{(m)}$, \begin{equation*} c_1 \, \omega_1[g_1,\ldots,g_k] + \ c_2 \, \omega_2[g'_1,\ldots,g'_{\ell}] = \omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k,g'_1,\ldots,g'_{\ell}]\,, \end{equation*} where $\omega = c_1 \, \omega_1[e^{(k+\ell)}_1,\ldots,e^{(k+\ell)}_k] + \ c_2 \, \omega_2[e^{(k+\ell)}_{k+1},\ldots,e^{(k+\ell)}_{k+\ell}]$
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Creed, Jeavons, Zivny 2013 (SICOMP), Lemma 6.4
assumptions: Let $C$ be a clone, and let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be weightings of $C$, of arity $k$ and $\ell$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: A weighted sum of superpositions of two weightings equals one superposition of a combined weighting built from projection superpositions.
nodes.label: lemma:sumofsuperpos

nodes.name: Pixley operations of type 1, 2, 3
nodes.statement: We call (ternary) operations corresponding to columns 5, 6, and 7 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} Pixley operations of type 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and will denote by P1 (P2 and P3) the Pixley operations of type 1 (2 and 3, respectively).

nodes.name: Semiprojections of type 1, 2, 3
nodes.statement: We call (ternary) semiprojections corresponding to columns 2, 3, and 4 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} semiprojections of type 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and will denote by S1 (S2 and S3) the semiprojections of type 1 (2 and 3, respectively).

nodes.name: Type of a $k$-ary semiprojection
nodes.statement: More generally, a $k$-ary semiprojection $f$ is called of type $1\leq i\leq k$ if equating any two inputs of $f$ results in $\ensuremath{e}^{(k)}_i$.

nodes.name: Cyclic permutation changes Pixley type
nodes.statement: For any Pixley operation $f$ of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ we can obtain, by (cyclically) permuting the arguments of $f$, Pixley operations of the other two types. For instance, if $f\in\mbox{P1}$ then we have $g\in\mbox{P2}$ and $h\in\mbox{P3}$, where $g(x,y,z)=f[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2]=f(z,x,y)$ and $h(x,y,z)=f[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1]=f(y,z,x)$.
assumptions: any Pixley operation $f$ of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$
conclusions:
by
(cyclically) permuting the arguments of $f$, Pixley operations of the other two
types

nodes.name: Related Pixley operations
nodes.statement: Two Pixley operations $f$ and $g$ of different types are called \emph{related} if there is a permutation $\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_3$ such that $f=g^\pi$. (Note that the requirement of $f$ and $g$ being of different types excludes the identity permutation $(1,2,3)$ and there are only other two permutations in $\mathrm{Cycl}_3$, namely $(2,3,1)$ and $(3,1,2)$.)
nodes.genus: Pixley operations $f$ and $g$ of different types

nodes.name: Related semiprojections
nodes.statement: Similarly, two semiprojections $f$ and $g$ of different types are called related if there is a permutation $\pi\in\mathrm{Cycl}_3$ such that $f=g^\pi$.

nodes.name: Types of sharp operations under cyclic permutations (Table 2)
nodes.statement: The following table, which can be verified using the definitions above, will be useful in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}. It lists the types of ternary sharp operations obtained by superposing a ternary sharp operation of an arbitrary type (columns in Table~\ref{tab:types}) with any of the three cyclic permutations of the three ternary projections (rows in Table~\ref{tab:types}).
conclusions:
It lists the types of ternary
sharp operations obtained by superposing a ternary sharp operation of an arbitrary
type (columns in Table~\ref{tab:types}) with any of the three cyclic permutations of the
three ternary projections (rows in Table~\ref{tab:types}).

nodes.name: Semiprojection and Pixley types permute differently
nodes.statement: Note that taking a semiprojection $f$ of type $i$ and a Pixley operation $g$ of type $i$, $f^\pi$ and $g^\pi$ can be of different types; e.g., if $f$ is a semiprojection of type $1$ and $g$ is a Pixley operation of type $1$ and $\pi=(2,3,1)$ then $f^\pi$ is a semiprojection of type $2$ and $g^\pi$ is a Pixley operation of type $3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: It suffices to consider the ternary case as the rest of the theorem follows from (the proof of) Theorem~\ref{thm:class1} and the fact that $W$ is a rigid core, which eliminates the first case of Theorem~\ref{thm:class1}. Let $W$ be a weighted clone containing a ternary positive weighting $\omega$ such that every $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ is sharp. (If some $f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)$ were not sharp then we could show, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:class1}, that the case~(1) holds.) We denote by $C$ the support clone of $W$. We assume that none of the cases (2a), (2b), (2c), (3) (with $k=3$) of the theorem applies as we would be done in any of these cases. By Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume that $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three ternary projections and thus \begin{equation} \sum_{f\in{\rm supp}(\omega)}\omega(f)\ =\ 3\,. \end{equation} Let $P_i\subseteq C$ be the Pixley operations of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ from $C$. Since $C$ is a clone we have \begin{equation} |P_1|\ =\ |P_2|\ =\ |P_3|\,. \end{equation} By Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we have for any three related Pixley operations $p_1\in P_1$, $p_2\in P_2$, and $p_3\in P_3$, \begin{equation} \omega(p_1)\ =\ \omega(p_2)\ =\ \omega(p_3)\,, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \sum_{p\in P_1} \omega(p)\ =\ \sum_{p\in P_2} \omega(p)\ =\ \sum_{p\in P_3} \omega(p)\,. \end{equation} We set $P=P_1\cup P_2\cup P_3$ to be the set of all Pixley operations from $C$ and $w(P)=\sum_{p\in P}\omega(p)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, the same holds for the three types of ternary semiprojections. In particular, we denote by $S_i\subseteq C$ the operations from $C$ that are semiprojections of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$. Since $C$ is a clone, we have \begin{equation} |S_1|\ =\ |S_2|\ =\ |S_3|\,. \end{equation} For any three related semiprojections $s_1\in S_1$, $s_2\in S_2$, and $s_3\in S_3$, \begin{equation} \omega(s_1)\ =\ \omega(s_2)\ =\ \omega(s_3)\,, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \sum_{s\in S_1} \omega(s)\ =\ \sum_{s\in S_2} \omega(s)\ =\ \sum_{s\in S_3} \omega(s)\,. \end{equation} We set $S=S_1\cup S_2\cup S_3$ to be the set of all semiprojections from $C$ and $w(S)=\sum_{s\in S}\omega(s)$. To simplify the presentation, we use the same notation for weightings, index sets, etc. in the following three steps since the steps are similar (but independent). Thus, for example, when one reads $J$ in Step II it refers to $J$ defined in Step II and not in Step I. \textbf{Step I}: Eliminating Pixley operations. We now show how to eliminate Pixley operations if needed, that is, assume $w(P)>0$ and thus some operations from $P$ are assigned positive weight. First assume that $\omega$ assigns positive weight to only Pixley operations, that is, ${\rm supp}(\omega)\subseteq P$. Hence $w(P)=3$. Take arbitrary $p_1,p'_1\in P_1$, $p_2,p'_2\in P_2$, and $p_3,p'_3\in P_3$. The following claims can be verified from the definitions: $p_1[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,p'_1]$ is a majority operation, $p_2[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,p'_1]=\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1$, and $p_3[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,p'_1]=\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2$. Consequently, $\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,p'_1]$ assigns weight $-1$ to $p'_1$, $+1$ to majority operations, and $0$ otherwise. Similarly, $\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,p'_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3]$ assigns weight $-1$ to $p'_2$, $+1$ to majority operations, and $0$ otherwise. Finally, $\omega[p'_3,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3]$ assigns weight $-1$ to $p'_3$, $+1$ to majority operations, and $0$ otherwise. Overall, the weighting \begin{equation} \mu\ =\ \omega+\sum_{p\in P_1}\omega(p)\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,p] +\sum_{p\in P_2}\omega(p)\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,p,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3] +\sum_{p\in P_3}\omega(p)\omega[p,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3] \end{equation} assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three ternary projections and weight $3$ to majority operations. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:sumofsuperpos}, the intermediate superpositions in~\eqref{eq:pixleyonly} can be improper as long as the resulting weighting $\mu$ is indeed a weighting. Thus $\mu\in W$ and case~(2a) of the theorem holds. Let assume that ${\rm supp}(\omega)\not\subseteq P$, that is, $\omega$ assigns positive weight not only to Pixley operations. Let $J=\{(p_1,p_2,p_3)\in P_1\times P_2\times P_3\:|\:\mbox{$p_1, p_2, p_3$ are related}\}$ and $\bar{J}=\{(\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3)\}\cup J$. We consider the following linear system: for all Pixley operations $p\in P$, \begin{equation} \sum_{(f,g,h) \in \bar{J}}x_{f,g,h}\omega[f,g,h](p)\ =\ 0\,. \end{equation} By Gordan's Theorem,~\eqref{eq:pixleyzero} has a nonzero nonnegative solution if and only if the following system of strict inequalities is unsatisfiable: for all $(f,g,h) \in \bar{J}$, \begin{equation} \sum_{p \in P}y_p\omega[f,g,h](p)\ >\ 0\,. \end{equation} Consider the case $\tuple{f,g,h}=\tuple{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}$. Then $\omega[f,g,h]=\omega$ and thus $\omega[f,g,h](p)=\omega(p)>0$ for all $p\in {\rm supp}(\omega)\cap P$, by the definition of $P$. Moreover, by~\eqref{eq:Pweights} \begin{equation} \sum_{p\in P}y_p\omega(p) \ =\ \sum_{p_1\in P_1}(y_{p_1}+y_{p_2}+y_{p_3})\omega(p_1)\,, \end{equation} where we denoted (with a slight abuse of notation) by $p_2$ and $p_3$ the related operations of $p_1$. For $\tuple{f,g,h} = \tuple{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}$ the LHS of~\eqref{eq:pixleygordan} is equal to~\eqref{eq:split}. Thus, for~\eqref{eq:pixleygordan} to hold in this case we must have at least one triple of related operations $\tuple{p_1,p_2,p_3} \in J$ with $y_{p_1} + y_{p_2} + y_{p_3} > 0$. Suppose $\tuple{p_1,p_2,p_3}\in J$ is chosen to maximise $y_{p_1} + y_{p_2} + y_{p_3}$. The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:pixleygordan} when $\tuple{f,g,h} = \tuple{p_1,p_2,p_3}$ is equal to \begin{equation} - y_{p_1} - y_{p_2} - y_{p_3} + \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s)\,, \end{equation} since $o[p_1,p_2,p_3]$ is equal to a Pixley operation only when $o$ is one of the three projections, which give the first three terms in~\eqref{eq:abc}, or a semiprojection, which gives the last term of~\eqref{eq:abc}, the sum over $S$. We have \begin{equation} \begin{split} \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s)\ =\ & \sum_{s_1\in S_1}y_{s_1[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s_1) + \sum_{s_2\in S_2}y_{s_2[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s_2) + \sum_{s_3\in S_3}y_{s_3[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s_3) \\ =\ & \sum_{\substack{\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}\in S_1\times S_2\times S_3\\s_1,s_2,s_3\mbox{ \scriptsize related}}}(y_{s_1[p_1,p_2,p_3]}+y_{s_2[p_1,p_2,p_3]}+y_{s_3[p_1,p_2,p_3]})\omega(s_1) \\ \leq\ & \frac{\omega(S)}{3}(y_{p_1}+y_{p_2}+y_{p_3}),\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the first equality follows from the definition of $S$; the second equality follows from fact that $s[p_1,p_2,p_3]$ is a Pixley operation of type $i$ given $s$ is a semiprojection of type $i$, where $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, and hence $\tuple{s_1[p_1,p_2,p_3],s_2[p_1,p_2,p_3],s_3[p_1,p_2,p_3]}$ is a triple of related Pixley operations given that $\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}$ is a triple of related semiprojections; and the last inequality follows from the definition of $w(S)$ and the choice of $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$. Combining~\eqref{eq:abc} and~\eqref{eq:S3}, we have \begin{equation} - y_{p_1} - y_{p_2} - y_{p_3} + \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[p_1,p_2,p_3]}\omega(s) \ \leq\ - y_{p_1} - y_{p_2} - y_{p_3} + \frac{w(S)}{3}(y_{p_1}+y_{p_2}+y_{p_3}) \ <\ 0\,, \end{equation} where the last strict inequality follows from $w(S)<3$ since $w(P)>0$ and~\eqref{eq:sum3}. Hence, \eqref{eq:pixleygordan} is unsatisfiable and, by Gordan's Theorem, \eqref{eq:pixleyzero} must have a nonzero nonnegative solution $x^*$. We finish Step~I by using $x^*$ to prove the existence of a weighting in $W$ that assigns zero weight to all Pixley operations. Let \begin{equation} \mu'=\sum_{(f,g,h) \in \bar{J}}x^*_{f,g,h}\omega[f,g,h]\,, \end{equation} be a weighted sum of superpositions of $\omega$. By the choice of $x^*$, $\mu'$ assigns zero weight to all Pixley operations. From the definition of $\bar{J}$, \begin{equation} \mu'\ =\ x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3]+\sum_{(f,g,h)\in J}x^*_{f,g,h}\omega[f,g,h]\,. \end{equation} We know that $x^*$ is nonzero and nonnegative. Note that $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}>0$ and $x^*_{f,g,h}=0$ for all $(f,g,h)\in J$ would contradict that $\mu'$ assigns zero weight to all Pixley operations. Let $(f,g,h)\in J$ and $i\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $o[f,g,h]$ is a Pixley operation of type $i$ if $o$ is a semiprojection of type $i$, $o[f,g,h]$ is a semiprojection of type $i$ if $o$ is a Pixley operation of type $i$, $o[f,g,h]$ is a majority operation if $o$ is a minority operation, and finally $o[f,g,h]$ is a minority operation if $o$ is a majority operation. It follows that $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}=0$ would contradict that $\mu'$ assigns zero weight all Pixley operations since Pixley operations of type $i$ would be assigned negative weight since $w(S)-3<0$ as $w(P)>0$. Thus $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}>0$ and $x^*_{f,g,h}>0$ for at least one $(f,g,h)\in J$. Consequently, $\mu'$ is a nonzero weighting that assigns zero weight to all Pixley operations. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:sumofsuperpos}, $\mu'\in W$. \textbf{Step II}: Eliminating semiprojections. We now show how to eliminate semiprojections if needed. If $\mu'$ obtained in Step I assigns positive weight to only semiprojections then we are in case (3) (with $k$=3) of the theorem. Thus let assume that $\mu'$ assigns positive weight to semiprojections and at least one majority or minority operation. By Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume the existence of a ternary weighting $\omega\in W$ which assigns weight -1 to all three projections (and thus assigns total positive weight 3). We will use the same notation for $S$, $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_3$ as before although note that the weighting $\omega$ is now different from the one we had before and throughout Step I. We have $w(S)<3$ and~\eqref{eq:Srelated},~\eqref{eq:Scard},~\eqref{eq:Sweights} still hold for $\omega$. We again use Gordan's Theorem to show that there exists a nonzero ternary weighting in $W$ that assigns positive weight to majority and minority operations only. Let $J=\{(s_1,s_2,s_3)\in S_1\times S_2\times S_3\:|\:\mbox{$s_1, s_2, s_3$ are related}\}$ and $\bar{J}=\{(\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3)\}\cup J$. We consider the following linear system: for all semiprojections $s\in S$, \begin{equation} \sum_{\tuple{f,g,h}\in \bar{J}}x_{f,g,h}\omega[f,g,h](s)\ =\ 0\,. \end{equation} By Gordan's Theorem,~\eqref{eq:semiprojzero} has a nonzero nonnegative solution if and only if the following system of strict inequalities is unsatisfiable: for all $(f,g,h) \in \bar{J}$, \begin{equation} \sum_{s \in S}y_s\omega[f,g,h](s)\ >\ 0\,. \end{equation} As in Step I, we can argue that~\eqref{eq:semiprojgordan} is unsatisfiable. Consider the case $\tuple{f,g,h}=\tuple{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}$. Then $\omega[f,g,h]=\omega$ and thus $\omega[f,g,h](s)=\omega(s)>0$ for all $s\in{\rm supp}(\omega)\cap S$, by the definition of $S$. Moreover, by~\eqref{eq:Sweights} \begin{equation} \sum_{s\in S}\omega(s)y_s \ =\ \sum_{s_1\in S_1}(y_{s_1}+y_{s_2}+y_{s_3})\omega(s_1)\,, \end{equation} where we denoted by $s_2$ and $s_3$ the related operations of $s_1$. Therefore, for \eqref{eq:semiprojgordan} to hold when $\tuple{f,g,h} = \tuple{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}$ we must have at least one triple of related semiprojections $\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3} \in J$ with $y_{s_1} + y_{s_2} + y_{s_3} > 0$. Suppose $\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}\in J$ is chosen to maximise $y_{s_1} + y_{s_2} + y_{s_3}$. The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:semiprojgordan} when $\tuple{f,g,h} = \tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}$ is equal to \begin{equation} - y_{s_1} - y_{s_2} - y_{s_3} + \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s)\,, \end{equation} since $o[s_1,s_2,s_3]$ is equal to a semiprojection only when $o$ is one of the three projections, which give the first three terms in~\eqref{eq:Sabc}, or a semiprojection, which gives the last term of~\eqref{eq:Sabc}, the sum over $S$. We have \begin{equation} \begin{split} \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s)\ =\ & \sum_{s_1\in S_1}y_{s_1[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s_1) + \sum_{s_2\in S_2}y_{s_2[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s_2) + \sum_{s_3\in S_3}y_{s_3[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s_3) \\ =\ & \sum_{\substack{\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}\in S_1\times S_2\times S_3\\s_1,s_2,s_3\mbox{\scriptsize related}}}(y_{s_1[s_1,s_2,s_3]}+y_{s_2[s_1,s_2,s_3]}+y_{s_3[s_1,s_2,s_3]})\omega(s_1) \\ \leq\ & \frac{\omega(S)}{3}(y_{s_1}+y_{s_2}+y_{s_3}),\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the first equality follows from the definition of $S$; the second equality follows from fact that $s[s_1,s_2,s_3]$ is a semiprojection of type $i$ given $s$ is a semiprojection of type $i$, where $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, and hence $\tuple{s_1[s_1,s_2,s_3],s_2[s_1,s_2,s_3],s_3[s_1,s_2,s_3]}$ is a triple of related semiprojections given that $\tuple{s_1,s_2,s_3}$ is a triple of related semiprojections; and the last inequality follows from the definition of $w(S)$ and the choice of $(s_1,s_2,s_3)$. Combining~\eqref{eq:Sabc} and~\eqref{eq:SS3}, we have \begin{equation} - y_{s_1} - y_{s_2} - y_{s_3} + \sum_{s \in S}y_{s[s_1,s_2,s_3]}\omega(s) \ \leq\ - y_{s_1} - y_{s_2} - y_{s_3} + \frac{w(S)}{3}(y_{s_1}+y_{s_2}+y_{s_3}) \ <\ 0\,, \end{equation} where the last strict inequality follows from $w(S)<3$. Hence, \eqref{eq:semiprojgordan} is unsatisfiable and, by Gordan's Theorem, \eqref{eq:semiprojzero} must have a nonzero nonnegative solution $x^*$. We finish Step~II by using $x^*$ to prove the existence of a weighting in $W$ that assigns zero weight to all semiprojections. Let \begin{equation} \mu=\sum_{(f,g,h) \in J}\omega[f,g,h]x^*_{f,g,h}\,, \end{equation} be a weighted sum of superpositions of $\omega$. By the choice of $x^*$, $\mu$ assigns zero weight to all semiprojections. From the definition of $\bar{J}$, \begin{equation} \mu\ =\ x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3]+\sum_{(f,g,h) \in J}x^*_{f,g,h}\omega[f,g,h]\,. \end{equation} We know that $x^*$ is nonzero and nonnegative. Note that $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}>0$ and $x^*_{f,g,h}=0$ for all $(f,g,h)\in J$ would contradict that $\mu'$ assigns zero weight to all semiprojections. Let $(s_1,s_2,s_3)\in J$ and $i\in\{1,2,3\}$. Then $o[s_1,s_2,s_3]$ is a semiprojection of type $i$ if $o$ is a semiprojection of type $i$, $o[s_1,s_2,s_3]$ is a majority operation if $o$ is a majority operation, and finally $o[s_1,s_2,s_3]$ is a minority operation if $o$ is a minority operation. (Note that we do not need to consider the case when $f$ is a Pixley operation as $\omega$ assigns zero weight to all Pixley operations.) It follows that $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}=0$ would contradict that $\mu$ assigns zero weight all semiprojections since semiprojections of type $i$ would be assigned negative weight since $w(S)-3<0$ as $\omega$ assigns positive weight to some majority or minority (or possibly both) operations. Thus $x^*_{\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_2,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_3}>0$ and $x^*_{f,g,h}$ for at least one $(f,g,h)\in J$. Consequently, $\mu$ is a nonzero weighting that assigns zero weight to all semiprojections. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:sumofsuperpos}, $\mu\in W$. \textbf{Step III}: Majority and minority operations. In Steps I and II, we have shown that any weighted clone $W$ with a positive ternary weighting contains a ternary weighting that assigns nonzero weight to semiprojections alone (case~(3) of the theorem with $k=3$), or a mix of majority and minority operations. Finally, we will show that if $W$ contains a weighting $\omega$ that assigns weight to majority and minority operations alone then $W$ also contains a weighting of one of the three types described in cases~(2a),~(2b), and~(2c) of the theorem. Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ denote the sets of majority and minority operations in the support of $\omega$. Suppose that $\omega$ assigns total weight $2+a$ to $M_1$ and total weight $1-a$ to $M_2$ for some $a > 0$. For each $f \in M_2$, we define $\mu_f = \omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,f]$, so $\mu_f$ assigns weight $a$ to $\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1$ and weight $-a$ to $f$. Note that $\mu_f$ is not a proper weighting, since $a > 0$. We obtain a weighting $\mu \in W$ which assigns positive weight to majority operations only as follows: \begin{equation} \mu = \omega + \sum_{f \in M_2}\frac{\omega(f)}{a}\mu_f\,. \end{equation} Similarly, suppose that $\omega$ assigns total weight $2-a$ to $M_1$ and total weight $1+a$ to $M_2$ for some $a>0$. For each $f\in M_1$, we define $\mu_f=\omega[\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1,f,f]$, so $\mu_f$ assigns weight $a$ to $\ensuremath{e}^{(3)}_1$ and weight $-a$ to $f$. We obtain a weighting $\mu \in W$ which assigns positive weight to minority operations only as follows: \begin{equation} \mu = \omega + \sum_{f \in M_1}\frac{\omega(f)}{a}\mu_f\,. \end{equation} In both cases $\mu\in W$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sumofsuperpos}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a symmetric ternary sharp weighting and use Gordan's theorem (LP duality) twice to eliminate Pixley operations and then semiprojections. Step III rebalances majority and minority weights to reach (2a), (2b) or (2c).
